text: It's easy to conflate Qiskit and IBM's quantum computers into one thing, but they're genuinely separate layers with a sharp line between them — one is free software you run yourself, the other is a cloud service with an account and usage limits.

The Qiskit SDK is the open-source Python library you installed last lesson. It runs entirely on your own machine — no account, no internet connection, no usage quota, and nothing you do with it leaves your computer unless you explicitly submit a job. The IBM Quantum Platform is IBM's cloud service, where real superconducting processors physically live, and where qiskit-ibm-runtime submits jobs to them. The two are connected — the SDK is the client you use to talk to the Platform — but they are not the same thing.

That account and region switcher in the Platform's own header is a detail that only exists once you're inside the cloud service. Nothing in the local SDK has an equivalent, because the SDK doesn't track an account or a region at all.

Every circuit-building and debugging skill through Chapter 4 of this course requires nothing from the Platform. AerSimulator is classical simulation running on your own CPU — no network call, no account, no risk of burning through a usage quota while you experiment and make mistakes. The one thing local simulation can't give you is a measurement from an actual physical device, with the real noise and hardware constraints that come with it — and that's the entire value proposition of the Platform.

IBM periodically adjusts the quotas on its free and open-plan access — how much execution time or how many jobs you get. Any specific number you read in a blog post or even an older version of this course's own materials can go stale, so check IBM's current pricing or plans page once it actually matters, which in practice is only once you reach Chapter 5.
Next lesson is where setup and context end and building begins: a single qubit, one Hadamard gate, and your first look at real measurement output.
